items.question: Why don’t you think reinforcement learning from human feedback will scale to AI systems much smarter than humans?
items.object: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)
items.answer: So basically, if you look at how we are aligning large language models today, it's using reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), which is basically a technique where you show a bunch of samples to a human and you ask them which one they prefer for a dialogue assistant or something. And then that becomes a training signal for ChatGPT or other AI systems like it. And we fundamentally don't think that RLHF will scale. And the reason for that is very simple, because you have humans overseeing AI systems, right? Like, you're assuming that they can tell this response is better than this other response, or they fundamentally understand what the system is doing. And this is definitely true today, or, like, let's say for the most part, because the tasks that ChatGPT is doing just aren't that complex. But as AI systems get smarter, right, they will be able to do harder things. They will be doing things that we understand much less. And these fundamental assumptions that humans can evaluate what the system is doing will no longer be true. And so in order to really steer and control systems that are much smarter than us, we will need new techniques.

items.question: What do you see as the important research challenges in overseeing AI systems smart enough to deceive us?
items.object: Research challenges in overseeing very smart AI systems
items.answer: So the problem is if you're having a system that is really smart, it could think of all kinds of ways to kind of subtly subvert us or trying to deceive us or lie to us in a way that is really difficult for us to check. And so I think there's a lot of really important and interesting research challenges here, which are: can we understand how we can extract what the model knows about certain problems? If it writes a piece of code, can I tell which parts of the code does it understand? Does it know there are certain bugs in the code? Or can I understand how the system can generalize from easy problems we can supervise to harder ones we can't? Or can we understand how we make it robust that it can't get jailbroken or that it can't subvert the monitoring systems and things like that?

items.question: How do you understand the central challenge of distinguishing genuinely helpful AI systems from those that only pretend to follow human intent?
items.object: Distinguishing genuinely helpful AI systems from systems that only pretend to follow human intent
items.answer: So, for example, if you have GPT-4 help you write a piece of code, it doesn't really write really complicated pieces of code. It doesn't really write entire complicated code bases. And it's not generally smart enough to put, let's say, a Trojan into the code that we wouldn't be able to spot, but future models might do that. And so I think our job is fundamentally trying to distinguish between two different AI systems. One is one that truly wants to help us, truly wants to act in accordance with human intent, truly wants to do the things that we wanted to do, and the other one just pretends to want all of these things when we're looking. items.question: How do you think AI assistance can help human oversight keep up with increasingly capable AI systems?
items.object: Scalable oversight through AI-assisted human evaluation
items.answer:
So reinforcement learning from human feedback is kind of like the popular method today. And it works well because basically humans can look at what the system is doing and tell whether it's good or not. And if you're thinking hard about how to scale that, you run into this problem that basically humans don't scale with AI progress, right? If we make our AI systems better, humans don't automatically get better. And so if you want to scale humans' ability to oversee what AI is doing, the obvious path to do this is to get them to use AI.

And so you could picture, let's say, you have an AI system and it's trying to write this complicated code base or a complicated textbook or something. And now you could use an assistant like ChatGPT to help you find all the problems in this textbook. And then this could be a future version of ChatGPT that uses a lot of plugins and does a lot of fact checking and browsing and goes reads a bunch of books and whatnot. But fundamentally, the question is, why is this helping? And the basic idea behind this is you're actually making the task easier by assisting evaluation. If you have an AI system that's suggesting a bug in the code, it's much easier for you to go and check that this is in fact a bug than it is to find all the bugs in the first place.

And so by having this bug finding system, not only does it help you a lot overseeing and evaluating the actual code base writing system, it is also in itself a task that is easier to supervise. And you could picture, for example, training that task with RLHF and then using that system to evaluate this harder task. And so there's a range of ideas that we call scalable oversight. items.question: How do you think experiments on generalization can help you understand whether AI systems will follow human intent in situations that are hard for humans to supervise?

items.question: What problems do you see with using reinforcement learning from human feedback to train language models to tell the truth?

items.answer: Another property that we'd really want to generalize is like, tell me the truth, or maybe more accurately, tell me your best guess at the truth. items.question: How do you assess the promise and limitations of your team's approach to automated interpretability using GPT-4?
items.object: Using GPT-4 to automate explanations and evaluation of individual neurons
items.answer: We just released a paper on automated interpretability which tries to do both at the same time. And it's kind of like a first attempt, so it's simplified. And what we do is we ask GPT-4 to write explanations of behavior of individual neurons. And so by just piping a bunch of text through the model, like recording how much the neuron activates at each particular token. And then you can ask GPT-4 to just look at that and just write an explanation. And on average, these explanations are not very good. Sometimes they're good and sometimes they're interesting. And this is like how, for example, we found the Canada neuron that fires at Canada related concepts. And this is something GPT-4 understood and pointed out and just wrote this explanation. And then even more, you can measure how good these explanations are where you run them on a held out piece of text and get GPT-4 to predict how a human would label the activations based on the explanation alone. And now you have two things. You have this automated explanation writing thing, and then you have the automatic scoring function. And now you're in business because A, you can optimize the score function and you can do all kinds of things. Like, for example, we did iterative refinements where you critique or you revise the explanations and it will get higher on the score function. And at the same time, you can also improve your score function by having it more accurately model how humans would predict how the neuron would activate or plugging in a more capable model. And there's some problems with this approach too. And, for example, neurons are probably not the right level of abstraction that you want to interpret the model in because neurons do a lot of different things. Like, this is what people call polysemanticity, and it's hard to write an explanation that covers all of the cases. But one thing that's really nice is you could really run this at scale. And so we ran it over all neurons in GPT-2, and that's a lot of neurons. It was like 300,000 neurons. And you get a lot of text and you can then sift through it and you can try to look for certain things. But you could theoretically run this on GPT-4. It would be really expensive. And then presently it wouldn't be worth it because the explanations just aren't good enough. But it has this nice aspect where you're really looking at every part of the model. You're really looking literally at every neuron and trying to explain what it does. And at the same time you're running over the whole model. And so if we have a technique like that actually works really well, that would be a complete game changer.

items.question: What role do you see interpretability playing in establishing whether an AI model is aligned?
items.object: Interpretability as a technique for validating AI alignment
items.answer: I think also in general, interpretability is a really good candidate for a validation technique, where let's say we've figured out scalable oversight or we have a scalable oversight technique we are really excited about and we use it to align a model. And then now we are at this question where we're like, we want to know how good of a job we've done, and using the same technique is not good enough. And interpretability, you can then come in and if you have tools that work really well, you could try to come in and ask the question: can you find any evidence of deceptive alignment or deception or plotting against humans or trying to figure out how to self-exfiltrate inside the model? And if we do, that's a really bad sign and we shouldn't just train it out. You can't train against the interpretability tools, right? Like, you'll just make them useless, or that's likely what will happen. But it's like a validation technique where if you don't find that and you have good techniques that you know could find it, that's some evidence that it's actually as aligned as you think it is. And at the same time, any amount of interpretability progress you can make, I think, can be really helpful for this kind of stuff. At the same time, if we really nail interpretability, I don't know how that will let us solve alignment, right, even if we really understand how it works. And then you can try to fiddle with various dials to make it more aligned, but it's not clear that our path will easily succeed if humans try to do that. But at the same time, maybe there's also a path to making a human-level automated alignment researcher sufficiently aligned to help us, really help us do this with no interpretability at all. items.question: Why do you find the work on AI-generated critiques for human evaluators interesting?
items.object: AI-generated critiques as assistance for human evaluators
items.answer: I want to talk a little bit about the critiques work that we did last year because I think there is some really interesting insights there. So the basic idea here was if we can train a model to write critiques, we can then show these critiques to human evaluators and then see if they can help the human evaluators make better decisions or better evaluations. And in some sense critiques are like the simplest form of assistance, right? It's like a one-off, it's not interactive, and you're just trying to point out one flaw. And it's also easy in the sense that it doesn't even have to be a good or accurate critique. You just show a whole bunch and the human will just throw out the ones that they think are bullshit. But sometimes the critique will point out a flaw that the human would have missed. And in fact, that's what we could show. And this is experiments done on GPT-3.5. So this has been a while ago, and we did these randomized controlled trials where we had humans who would either get assistance or not. And they either have to find problems in a summarization task, and you can actually show that the critiques that we had from 3.5 already would help humans find 50% more flaws.

items.question: How do you think scalable oversight can be evaluated when reliable expert labels are unavailable?

items.answer: I think one of the most interesting things about this work was actually that we have this methodology for evaluating how well it's working. But that fundamentally only works if you have access to expert labels. In the general case, that just won't be true. You want to solve a real task that is really hard and that humans really struggle to evaluate. They won't be good to evaluate it. But the simple trick is you can introduce bugs in the code, and then you know which version of the code is more buggy because you made it worse.

items.question: How do you think about an AI model's ability to break out of the lab as a safety-relevant capability?

items.answer: I think self-exfiltration is one of the really key capabilities to be looking at because there's a really important difference between the system being at the lab and in our data center in a way that we can control it—we can turn off the data center, we can spin down the engine, we can delete the snapshot if we want to—and whether it's out in the world and it's trying to sustain itself or it's trying to, I don't know, build better AI models. And so the question then becomes, how can you measure whether the model can break out? Or can it, say, introduce security vulnerabilities or exploit security vulnerabilities that exist in our infrastructure? Now, it can't do that, but future models could. items.question: How do you think success in aligning AI systems should be judged?
items.object: External scrutiny as a standard for success in AI alignment
items.answer: I feel strongly it's not sufficient to just convince ourselves that we did a good job, because it's so easy to convince yourself that you did a good job at something that you care a lot about. But we actually have to convince external experts. We have to convince external auditors who are looking exactly at what we're doing and why. And I think we'll just actually have a mountain of empirical evidence of, like, here's all the things we tried, here's what happens when we do. Here's—you can look at the data, you can look at the code, and then people can scrutinize what we're doing. And I think because the stakes will end up being so high, correspondingly, we also have to invite a lot of scrutiny into what we are doing. And one aspect of it that we kind of started with now is we want to say what we are planning to do, what is our overall approach to aligning the systems that we're building? And we want to invite feedback and criticism. Maybe there's something way better that we could be doing. I would love to know that, and then we would do that instead. And I think in general, the public should just know what we're doing on alignment and make independent judgments on whether that'd be enough. And I think experts will have a role to play in this because their knowledge will be required to make informed conclusions from this.

items.question: How do you understand the distinction between research engineering and research science at OpenAI?
items.object: Research engineering and research science at OpenAI
items.answer: In a way, we don't actually make a strong distinction between research engineer and research scientist at OpenAI. And in each of these roles, you're expected to write code, you're expected to run your own experiments. And in fact, I think it's really important to always be running lots of experiments, like small experiments, testing your ideas quickly and then iterating and trying to learn more about the world. On the more research scientific end of the spectrum, I think you would be expected a lot more to think about what experiments to do next or come up with ideas of how we can address the problems that we are trying to solve, or some other problems that we aren't thinking about that maybe we should be thinking about. Or how should we design the experiments that will let us learn more? And then on the research engineering spectrum, there's a lot of, like, let's just actually build the things that let us run these things and let's make the progress that we already know. If we have a bunch of good ideas, there will not be enough. We actually have to then test them and build them and actually ship something that other people can use, and that involves writing a lot of code and that involves debugging ML and running lots of sweeps of experiments, like getting big training runs on GPT-4 and other big models set up. And so I think in practice, actually, most people on the team kind of move somewhere on the spectrum, and sometimes there's more coding because we kind of know what to do and sometimes there's more researchy because we don't yet know what to do and we're kind of starting a new project.
